Binance Details $6.34B Hack: Fake Job Interviews Used to Plant Malware, Internal AI Tool Exploited Binance released an initial report on its October 29 hack, revealing that attackers used fake job interviews and malware to compromise an engineer's device in September. They later exploited an internal AI tool to gain access to wallet engineers, then used stolen credentials to compromise a wallet signing service and abuse Ethereum's EIP-7702 authorization mechanism. Binance said withdrawal suspensions alone could not stop the malicious on-chain authorizations, which required a separate revocation process. Of the $6.34 billion in affected assets, approximately $2.85 billion has been frozen or intercepted. Binance said 98% of affected token assets had been replenished as of October 31, with sufficient funds set aside to cover all losses. The investigation remains ongoing. — link

Binance Hack Timeline: How Attackers Compromised Three Engineers to Access Wallet Signing Service WuBlockchain mapped the attack timeline based on Binance’s preliminary investigation. In June, Wallet DevOps Engineer A downloaded a tampered Homebrew installer while setting up an AI coding tool. Although Binance detected the incident, replaced the device and rotated credentials, information about the engineer and colleagues was exposed. In September, Engineer B downloaded a malicious code repository during a fake job interview, compromising his work computer. On October 20, attackers used the compromised device and an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineers A and C, discovering a container deployment permission token on A’s computer. On October 29, they accessed C’s computer, used credentials stolen from A to deploy a container and execute a malicious script, and ultimately initiated unauthorized asset transfers through Binance’s internal wallet signing service. — link

Analyst: Suspected North Korean Hackers Moved $1.46M via Jupiter Lend and Circle Bridge; Jupiter Says Funds Remain Traceable On-chain analyst @FabianoSolana reported that suspected North Korean hackers moved approximately $1.46 million through Jupiter Lend and Circle’s cross-chain bridge. Funds from an FBI-flagged Solana wallet (AffzFD) were routed through roughly 35 intermediary wallets, consolidated, and deposited into Jupiter Lend before a new wallet withdrew a similar amount minutes later. The funds were then swapped into USDC, bridged through Noble and dYdX, and returned to Solana. The analyst reported 16 outbound transfers totaling $1,463,410 and 19 inbound transfers totaling $1,463,400, with no funds frozen. Jupiter COO Kash Dhanda clarified that the attackers only deposited and withdrew funds through Jupiter Lend, unlike an earlier Aave incident involving borrowing non-freezable assets against stolen stablecoins. He said the funds remained fully traceable through LP tokens, with wallet associations preserved, and that Jupiter’s security team monitored the activity in real time. As of publication, Circle had not publicly addressed the transfers or explained why the funds were not frozen. — link

Major Developer Documentation Platform GitBook Hit by AI Agent-Driven Attack, Crypto Projects' Docs Affected GitBook reported that attackers used AI agents to gain unauthorized access to some of its infrastructure credentials at 1:00 p.m. EST on November 2. The company detected and blocked the attack, temporarily suspending some services. Potentially exposed data includes integration tokens, Git Sync secrets, API tokens, and visitor questions submitted to GitBook Assistant. No evidence of content modification has been found. GitBook rotated all infrastructure credentials and secrets, revoked all customer API tokens, and advised users to rotate third-party credentials and re-authenticate GitBook MCP connections. By 10:21 a.m. EST on November 3, its app, API, and published docs were accessible again, though some services remained degraded. A full post-incident report is planned. Previously, trade[XYZ] reported unauthorized activity involving its GitBook documentation, which it later restored, and warned users against clicking links during the investigation. PancakeSwap temporarily took its documentation site offline as a precaution following the GitBook security incident and redirected documentation links to its official homepage. — link
